chapters.label: Prologue
chapters.title: The Watch
chapters.html:
I am sitting here with a pocket watch in my hand.

It is small and heavy and worn smooth at the edges, the way metal gets when it has lived for years in a man's pocket and been taken out a thousand times to check the hour. I open the case. Inside there is one word: Edinburgh. That is almost all he left me.

The watch belonged to my grandfather. The family says he carried it across the Atlantic in 1929, and he carried it for the rest of his life, and he died before I was born. I am named for him. And for most of my life I knew almost nothing about him: a name, a few photographs, a grave in Cranston, a handful of stories my mother told about a quiet man who dressed shop windows and loved to read.

Who was he? Where did he come from? Why was there only one word inside his watch?

So I went searching for him, back through time, through ships' manifests and city streets and a century of other people's lives, until, in my own mind and heart, I brought him back to life.

This is what I found.

On the last day of his life, Rhode Island was icing over.

The storm came up the coast in the dark. All that day Providence had fog, snow, sleet and rain.

Providence was changing. The mills that had made Rhode Island rich were closing or moving south, and downtown, where he had dressed windows before the war, was losing its shoppers to the new plazas out on the highways.

That day, at St. Joseph's Hospital, Laurence Brown Douglas died. He was fifty-three years old. The illness had been brief. My mother remembered that the family did not know he had lung cancer until he was in the hospital.

He lived at 644 River Avenue, in the Elmhurst section of Providence, with his wife, Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas, a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. Before he went into business for himself he had dressed windows for Bond Stores, the clothing chain, in San Francisco and been its display manager in Pittsburgh. In the last years of his life he was dressing windows on his own account; the city directory of 1960 listed him as displayman for Carter's Men Store in Pawtucket.

On Saturday the Pawtucket Times ran his obituary on page three. It said he had been born in Edinburgh, Scotland. It named his parents as the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. It said that for the past fifteen years he had dressed windows for Pawtucket firms. It listed his wife, three daughters, and a sister in Chicago.

Most of it was true as far as it went. None of it told how he began.

He had been born in Edinburgh fifty-three years earlier, to a young woman of twenty-one from the village of Quothquan. She was not Elizabeth Douglas, and she did not give him the name Douglas. On the day his birth was written into the register, his name was Lawrence Brown.

He would carry that name across the Atlantic. He would carry another one through a Scottish schoolroom, a Chicago wedding and a federal courthouse in Pittsburgh. By the end he had put the two together, Laurence Brown Douglas, and kept them both. The records spell his first name both ways. This book calls him Laurence, the spelling he used as a man, and keeps Lawrence wherever a record wrote it that way.

This is the story of how he came by those names, and of the people who gave them to him.

It begins in the Scottish Borders, more than a century before that March day, with a family of farm laborers who owned nothing but their skill.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The Ploughmen
chapters.html:
Every life has a beginning before it begins. His began in a ploughed field, behind a pair of horses, on land that no one in his family had ever owned.

The Browns worked other men's land.

They lived through one of the great upheavals in the history of the Scottish countryside. In the century before 1850 the old run-rig farms, worked in common by whole townships, had been swept away and replaced by large enclosed farms let to single tenants, who paid rent to the laird and hired labor by the half-year. The cottars and small tenants who had once held a scrap of land of their own became landless hired men. A ploughman of the 1840s owned his skill, his strength and perhaps a chest of clothes. He did not own the roof over his head; the cottage came with the job, and when the job ended at the term he loaded his family and furniture onto a farm cart and moved.

He was paid partly in money and partly in kind: so many bolls of oatmeal, so many hundredweights of potatoes, a row in the potato field, the keep of a cow, coals carted from the nearest pit. Oatmeal porridge in the morning, brose at noon, potatoes and milk at night: it was a hard diet, but in the Lowlands it was regular, and the Lowland farm worker was spared the famine that the potato blight of 1846 brought to the Highlands and to Ireland.

They came from the high, bare sheep country of Peeblesshire, in the Scottish Borders, where the Tweed rises in the hills above Tweedsmuir and runs east through Stobo and Lyne toward the market town of Peebles. William Brown, born about 1835, was a ploughman. He walked behind a pair of horses, turning the stony ground for oats and turnips, and he moved from farm to farm as the hiring fairs and the term days dictated.

His wife was Agnes McGarth, born about 1840 at Tweedsmuir. The McGarths were hill people. In 1851 the census found her father, Tweedie McGarth, about thirty-eight, and her mother, Jane, about forty-one, a woman from Wamphray in Dumfriesshire, with a house full of children: Jane, Agnes, James Tweedie, Sarah, Ann and Janet. The family's names would outlast the family. "Tweedie" and "McGarth" were passed down as middle names for three generations, a way of remembering who you came from when you owned nothing else to leave.

William and Agnes Brown had at least ten children. There was William, about 1859. There was Lawrence Tweedie Brown, born on September 14, 1860, in Peebles. There was George, born on July 18, 1862. Then Alexander, Jane, John, James Tweedie, a daughter Agnes born at Stobo about 1875, Thomas, and Tweedie McGarth Brown about 1880. In 1871 the census found Lawrence, ten, and George, eight, living in the same household.

Two of those boys matter to this story.

Lawrence Tweedie Brown would grow up, marry a woman named Isabella Graham from Cambusnethan, raise a family at Traquair and Sanquhar, and eventually settle in Quebec. He died in 1943. Forty-seven years after his own birth, his niece would give his name to her son.

George was that niece's father. He became a ploughman like his own father. He did not live long enough to become anything else.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Agnes
chapters.html:
She was born in a ploughman's cottage, a week before Christmas, in the dark of a Border winter.

George Brown married Christina Henderson on Friday, June 1, 1883, in the parish of Libberton, at Quothquan, in the upper valley of the River Clyde. He was twenty. She was twenty-three.

Rural Scotland in the 1880s was emptying. Machines were coming onto the farms: horse-drawn reapers and binders, threshing mills driven by steam. Each one did the work of several men. Every year thousands of farm servants left for the coalfields of Lanarkshire, the shipyards and engine shops of Glasgow, or the emigrant ships for Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Those who stayed were better paid than their fathers had been, and better fed, but they were still hired by the half-year and still lived in houses they did not own.

The Hendersons were Libberton people. Christina's father, Alexander Henderson, born about 1830, and her mother, Jane Robb, had raised a family there: Christina, born on March 19, 1860, then Jane, Janet, David, and in about 1876 a late son, Andrew. The parish was farm country on the north side of the Clyde, four miles from the market town of Biggar, under a bald round hill called Quothquan Law. Across the river, filling the southwest sky, stood Tinto, the red hill of Clydesdale, with a great cairn on its summit that people said had been carried up stone by stone as penance.

Eleven weeks after the wedding, at twenty past eight on the morning of Saturday, August 18, 1883, Christina gave birth to a daughter at Quothquan. She went to the registrar herself on September 5 and gave the child's name as Mary Henderson Brown.

By the winter of 1885 George had found work across the county line, at Edston, a farm in the parish of Lyne, a few miles west of Peebles. The farm cottages there, low and stone-built with slate roofs, still stand along the road. At half past two in the afternoon on Friday, December 18, 1885, Christina gave birth to a second daughter.

On the last day of the year George registered her at Peebles. The registrar, George Morison, wrote the entry: Agnes McGarth Brown, female, born December eighteenth, 2h 30m p.m., at Edston, Peebles. Father, George Brown, ploughman. Mother, Christina Brown, maiden surname Henderson. Parents married 1883 June 1st, Libberton, Lanark. George signed as father.

He gave his daughter his own mother's name, Agnes McGarth.

George Brown died at Edston at half past one in the morning on Monday, April 5, 1886, when his younger daughter was three and a half months old. He was twenty-three years old. His death register is the document that names his own parents, William Brown, ploughman, and Agnes Brown, maiden surname McGarth.

Christina was left a widow at twenty-six, with a girl of two and a half and a baby of three and a half months. She took them home to Libberton.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Cottages at Quothquan
chapters.html:
In a row of six stone cottages that the village called Castle, a little girl of five was growing up among old men and widows.

On the road out of Quothquan village, past the smithy, there was a row of six crofters' cottages that the village called Castle.

For a girl of five like Agnes, the world was the length of the village road. Children walked to school, came home to help in the house and the fields, and by twelve or thirteen were expected to start earning. A farm laborer's daughter could expect to go into service, in a farmhouse kitchen or a big house, while she was still in her early teens.

In the first cottage lived John Mather, a crofter of seventy, and his wife, Margaret. In the second lived George Weir, seventy-five, the parish mole catcher, and his wife, Jane. In the third lived the widow Ann Archibald, fifty-four, with her daughter Mary, twenty-seven, her son Alexander, twenty, who broke stones for the county roads, and her son John, seventeen, a farm servant. In the fourth, alone, lived Janet Paterson, seventy-eight, on the parish roll as a pauper. In the sixth lived old Christina Henderson, ninety-four, living on her own means with her daughter and a granddaughter.

The fifth house was crowded. It was the home of Jane Henderson, fifty-six, Christina Brown's mother, a crofter born in Carnwath. With her lived her daughter Jane, twenty-seven, a dressmaker; her son Andrew, a schoolboy; and a young farm laborer of eighteen named James Parker.

James Parker had been born in Biggar. He had come into the Henderson house as a small boy, and the census had a word for what he was. In 1881, when he was eight and at school, the enumerator wrote him down as "Adopted Son". In 1891 he was "Adopted". His marriage register later named Benjamin Parker and Jane Lawson as his parents.

On the night of Sunday, April 5, 1891, the census taker found two more children in the fifth house: Jane Henderson's granddaughters, Mary Brown, seven, and Agnes Brown, five.

They were there because their mother was dead. Christina Brown had died at Quothquan on February 10, 1891, eight weeks before the census. She was thirty. Her name was cut into the Henderson family stone.

The year was not finished with the row. On June 8, 1891, the girls' grandmother, Jane Henderson, died too. Twelve days later, on June 20, the Archibalds buried their son John, eighteen.

So by midsummer of 1891, Agnes Brown was five and a half years old and had lost her father, her mother and the grandmother who had taken her in. What she had left was her sister, her uncle Andrew, her aunt Jane, and the boy the family called adopted.

Agnes grew up in a household where a child who was not born to it could be taken in and kept. Twenty-one years later, a Dunfermline school clerk would write the same word, Adopted, beside her own son's name.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Shieldhill
chapters.html:
A rich man bought the land under the village, and the village began to change.

In 1898 the land under the village changed hands.

For generations the Chancellor family had owned the Shieldhill estate, a rambling mansion built around an old tower above Quothquan, and with it the village and its cottages. The Chancellors buried their dead in the ruined old kirk at Quothquan, which they had taken as a family burial place around 1780. In 1898 they sold to Nathaniel Dunlop, a Glasgow shipowner of the Allan Line and chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. Dunlop rebuilt Huntfield Place, turning six houses into four, and enlarged the smith's house. He was rich, Presbyterian and energetic. In 1903 he and his daughter, Miss Ellen Dunlop, put up Shieldhill Hall in the village, a cross-shaped hall of corrugated iron with timber gables and an open porch, for evening services. It still stands.

Money from the Atlantic paid for the new Shieldhill. The Allan Line, which Nathaniel Dunlop had served for half a century, ran steamers from Glasgow to Quebec and Montreal and carried tens of thousands of Scottish emigrants to Canada. The same ships that paid for the laird's improvements would carry the village's children away.

By the census of March 31, 1901, the Castle row had new names. The enumerator came first to Gean Tree Cottages. Gean is the Scots word for the wild cherry, a tree that flowers white in April and ripens its small dark fruit in July. In one lived Mary Archibald, thirty-five, a sewing mistress. In the other lived James Grossart, eighty, a road surfaceman born at Carstairs, with his granddaughter Marion, twenty-two.

Next came Lime Tree Cottage, and the Hendersons.

The head of the house was now Andrew Henderson, twenty-five, a groom. Long after he was gone the village would remember "Andrew Henderson, late of Lime Tree" as a poet and a keeper of bees. James Parker, twenty-eight, still lived with him, no longer called adopted but a boarder, and working now as a gamekeeper. With them were Andrew's two nieces: Mary Brown, seventeen, and Agnes Brown, fifteen.

There was no grown woman left in the house. The aunt, Jane the dressmaker, had gone.

Up the hill, Shieldhill House stood nearly empty on census night. Dunlop was at his house in Govan. The estate was kept by resident staff: servants, gardeners and keepers. Mary Archibald's brother Alexander, thirty, was now the domestic gardener there. At the neighboring estate of Huntfield the gamekeeper, Robert Arthur, lived at the lodge. Another keeper, Robert Clarkson, lived at Cormiston.

James Parker stayed in the district. By 1911 he was married, with three children, and keeping game at Shieldhill Mains.

Agnes, at fifteen, was a girl of the row with no parents and no money. For a girl like that in Upper Clydesdale the likeliest work was service. By the summer of 1907 the register would call her a domestic servant.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Lizzie
chapters.html:
She was four years old when her mother sailed for the other side of the world without her.

Thirty miles away, on the southern edge of Edinburgh, lived the woman who would raise Agnes Brown's son. She had begun life much as he would, raised by others.

The south side of Edinburgh in the 1870s was not the city of the guidebooks. Beyond the Meadows and the new villas of Grange and Newington, the road ran out through Liberton and Gilmerton into a country of coal pits, limeworks and miners' rows. Men went down shafts under the fields to cut coal for the city's fires; women and girls worked at the pithead and in the fields; children worked as soon as they could. The Old Town itself, a few miles to the north, was among the most crowded places in Europe. Whole families lived in single rooms in the tall tenements off the High Street and the Cowgate, and the Improvement Act of 1867 had only begun to pull down the worst closes.

Elizabeth Millar McDonald was born on May 31, 1874, at Liberton. Her mother, Ann McDonald, was about twenty.

Two years later, on July 28, 1876, Ann married a laborer named Robert Alexander Hope at 33 Regent Park Square in Glasgow. Robert Hope had been born at Rigg, near Gretna, on July 14, 1852. His mother's name was Elizabeth Millar.

Emigration offered a way out, and in the 1870s New Zealand wanted settlers badly. Its government paid assisted passages for working families from Britain, and thousands of Scots took them, in sailing ships that took about three months to reach Otago and Canterbury. In 1878 Ann and Robert Hope sailed. Their son, John Rakaia Hope, was born at sea on September 26, 1878, and was named for the emigrant ship. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa and raised four more children there. Ann died at Cross Creek in 1915. Robert died at Pukekohe in 1930.

They did not take Lizzie. She was four.

She was raised by her grandparents, John McDonald, a man of the Gilmerton district, and his wife, Janet, born Janet Page. In 1881 the census found them on the Main Road at Gilmerton: John, fifty-two; Janet, fifty-two; their grown son George; a daughter, Janet; a son, Alexander; and Elizabeth, six, a scholar, entered as "Grandchild".

At sixteen she was in service. On the night of the 1891 census she was living in as a general domestic servant at 14 Wilson Road, Liberton, in the house of a Robert and Mary Dryder and their four small sons, the youngest eight months old. Another servant, Catherine Davidson, twenty-eight, lived in with her.

Like her mother, and like the girl in Clydesdale whose son she would raise, Lizzie McDonald was a servant.

On June 9, 1899, at 34 St Patrick Square in Edinburgh, she married Robert Douglas, by the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. The marriage register gives her age as twenty-four, a domestic servant living at 4 Hatton Place. He was twenty-three, a saw miller of 29 St Leonard's Terrace, the son of Archibald Douglas, a forester, and Isabella Douglas, born Isabella Gray. Robert had been born on May 8, 1876, at 9 Canon Street in Edinburgh, when his father was a traveller for a wood merchant. His parents had married in January 1863 in the parish of Newton, on the southeastern edge of the city, close to Liberton and Gilmerton, the country Lizzie came from. The Douglases, like the McDonalds, were Edinburgh people. For her own parents Lizzie gave the names of the grandparents who had raised her, John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. One of the two witnesses was Janet Page Moodie. Within two years Robert was working as a stone machineman, a skilled worker who cut and dressed stone by machine. On April 29, 1900, Lizzie gave birth to a daughter and named her Janet Page Douglas, after the grandmother who had raised her.

On census night, March 31, 1901, the young family lived at 5 Beaumont Place, in the tenements of Newington on Edinburgh's south side: Robert, twenty-four; Lizzie, twenty-six; and Janet, eleven months.

Family information says that Robert and Lizzie had a second daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, named for Robert's mother, and that she died as an infant.

There is no evidence that the Douglases of Beaumont Place and the Browns of Lime Tree Cottage had ever heard of each other.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: The Autumn of 1906
chapters.html:
It happened in the year of the harvest heat wave, in the farm country of the upper Clyde. Who the father was, no record tells.

In the Upper Ward of Lanarkshire a servant's year turned on two days. Whitsunday, fixed by law at May 28, and Martinmas, fixed at November 28, were the term days. On those days engagements ended and began, wages were paid out for the half-year, and servants who were moving on carried their boxes out to a cart. A girl hired at Whitsunday usually lived in, ate in her employer's kitchen, and was paid at Martinmas. The government's Labour Gazette put the going rate for women farm servants in the southwest of Scotland at seven to ten pounds a half-year, with board. In 1906 it noted that women willing to go into service were hard to find.

Agnes Brown turned twenty in December 1905. Where she worked in 1906 is not recorded.

The summer ended in a heat wave. In the first days of September the afternoons across the south and east of Scotland went above eighty degrees.

The harvest stood in that heat. In the fields of the upper Clyde the oats were cut and set up in stooks to dry. Partridge shooting opened on September 1, and on the estates around Quothquan the keepers were out with the guns.

Somewhere in those weeks, between about the first week of September and the middle of October 1906, Agnes Brown conceived a child. She was twenty.

On the farms of the Upper Ward the young people still met at the feeing fairs, the harvest dances and the kirk door. The bicycle had given country boys and girls a freedom their parents had never had: a farm lad could ride ten miles to a dance on a Saturday night and be back for the morning milking.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Road to Edinburgh
chapters.html:
Her son would be born in the capital, thirty miles from home.

Whitsunday 1907 fell on a Tuesday. It was a cold day for the end of May, with an east wind off the North Sea. By then her child was due within weeks. A servant in that condition rarely kept a place where she lived in. Whether she left at the term, or before it, no one wrote down.

Agnes's son would be born in Edinburgh, in the middle of June.

Quothquan had no station. The nearest was Thankerton, across the Clyde, about a mile and a half by road. The railway had come through in 1848. The Carlisle expresses ran through without stopping; the local trains stopped. On a timetable from 1900 a morning train left Thankerton at 8:35 and reached Edinburgh at 9:40, and an afternoon train left at 2:35 and arrived at 3:55. At the parliamentary rate of a penny a mile, the third-class fare would have come to about two shillings and eightpence for the thirty-two miles: for a country servant, something like half a week's wages.

The line ran north up the Clyde valley to Carstairs Junction, where it divided for Glasgow and Edinburgh, then climbed northeast onto the moor, past Carnwath, where Agnes's grandmother had been born, past Auchengray and Cobbinshaw, where it ran beside the reservoir that fed the Union Canal, and past Harburn and Midcalder. Then it came down into the farmland of Midlothian, with the long ridge of the Pentland Hills to the south, past Curriehill and Slateford, where the canal crossed the Water of Leith on its aqueduct, and into the city.

The Caledonian line ended at Princes Street Station, at the west end of Princes Street. Lauriston Place lay about three-quarters of a mile to the south. It was a street of institutions and small shops: Chalmers Hospital at number 55; the Lauriston Place United Free church at 77; the Royal Maternity Hospital at 79, with its own telephone line, number 837.

The Home's own case records have not been found. Whether Agnes Brown spent her last weeks there is not known. She was the kind of young woman it was founded for.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Born at Nine O'Clock
chapters.html:
At nine o'clock on a summer evening, in a hospital that took in women who had nowhere else to go, a servant from the country gave birth to a son.

The Royal Maternity Hospital had been built in 1879 as a memorial to Sir James Young Simpson, the Edinburgh physician who first used chloroform to ease childbirth. It had the look of a seventeenth-century Scottish town house, with crow-stepped gables and a square corner tower.

The Royal Maternity Hospital was one of the places where that was beginning to change. Its wards were a teaching ground for the medical students of the university, and one of its physicians, Dr. John William Ballantyne, was campaigning for something almost nobody yet offered: care for mothers before their babies were born.

In 1907 the hospital was crowded. It delivered about 425 women a year in its own wards, more than one a day, and sent its doctors and pupil midwives out to nearly six hundred more in their homes. Its matron was Miss Edward. Four physicians took charge in turn, a quarter of the year each, among them Professor Sir John Halliday Croom and Dr. Freeland Barbour. Most ordinary deliveries were done by the house surgeons, the students and the pupil midwives. A Biblewoman visited the wards. So did a Ladies' Committee. Most of the women in the beds were servants, farm workers and shop girls.

Friday, June 14, 1907, was a mild, dull day, overcast and still. Britain did not yet keep summer time, and in Edinburgh the sun set at about nine.

At nine o'clock that evening, Agnes Brown gave birth to a son.

Overnight the drizzle came on. Mothers were usually kept about ten days, and the week that followed was cool and showery.

Less than nine years later, a German airship would drop its bombs on Lauriston Place.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: His First Name
chapters.html:
She had twenty-one days to register him. She did it on the twentieth.

On Thursday, July 4, 1907, the twentieth day, Agnes Brown registered her son at the office of the registrar for the district of St Giles, at 24 Forrest Road. At Leith it was a raw, gray day for July: fifty degrees at eight in the morning, a steady east-northeast breeze off the sea, overcast, with passing showers. The Leith station recorded less than an hour and a half of sunshine all day.

The registrar was R. D. Robertson.

Name: Lawrence Brown. Born 1907, June fourteenth, 9 h. 0 m. p.m., Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh. Sex: M. In the column for the father's name and occupation there was nothing at all. Below it: Agnes Brown, Domestic Servant (domicile Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar). Informant: Agnes Brown, Mother. Registered 1907, July 4th, at Edinburgh. R. D. Robertson, Registrar.

The name she gave him was not her own father's. Her father had been George. She gave her son the same first name as her uncle, Lawrence Tweedie Brown, her father's elder brother; in the family it was understood that he was named for him.

For her domicile she did not give Lime Tree, the cottage where the census had found her in 1901. She was living at Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

She signed the register as his mother, Agnes Brown, and registered him as Lawrence Brown.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: Gean Cottage
chapters.html:
On July 4, 1907, three weeks after her son was born, Agnes Brown gave the registrar in Edinburgh her home address: Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

She did not give Lime Tree Cottage, the house where she had grown up and where her uncle was head of the household. She was living a few doors along the same row. To understand why, you have to know whose house it was.

In 1891 the census enumerator called the row of cottages below Shieldhill "Castle." Later its houses took the names of trees, among them Gean Tree and Lime Tree.

When Agnes came to her grandmother's cottage in the row in 1891, at five, the Archibalds lived a few doors along: the widow Ann Archibald; her daughter Mary, twenty-seven; and her sons Alexander, who broke stones for the roads, and John, who died that June at eighteen (Chapter 3). Mary Archibald was among the first grown women Agnes knew outside her own family.

The 1890s took the Archibald house apart. On December 10, 1897, Ann Archibald died; her name is cut on the family stone. That left Mary in the cottage. And at about the same time, Mary Archibald had a child of her own.

Her gravestone, raised many years later at Biggar, records a daughter, Annie P. R., who died on November 22, 1992, at the age of ninety-four. Annie was born, then, about 1897 or 1898. The man Mary later married, John Cuthbertson, is named on the same stone as "Father." If Mary was not yet married when her daughter was born, then ten years before Agnes, in the same row of cottages, the woman a few doors along had faced the very thing Agnes would face.

On census night in 1901 Mary Archibald, a sewing mistress, was living alone at Gean Tree. Her daughter, about three, was not with her. Her brother Alexander, the stonebreaker of 1891, was now the domestic gardener at Shieldhill House, up the hill. A few doors along, at Lime Tree, Agnes, fifteen, lived with her uncle Andrew, her sister, Mary Brown, and James Parker (Chapter 4). Her grandmother was dead and her aunt Jane had gone. There was no grown woman under that roof.

So who was there to be a mother to her? Not the men at Lime Tree. The grown woman in that row who had known Agnes since she was five, who had buried a brother and a mother of her own, who taught needlework and had a child of her own living elsewhere, was Mary Archibald.

Then the records go quiet for five years.

In the autumn of 1906 Agnes, twenty, conceived a child. On June 14, 1907, her son was born in Edinburgh, and on July 4 she registered him, with the column for his father's name left empty. Her home, she told the registrar, was Gean Cottage.

In 1901 Agnes was living at Lime Tree with her uncle, her sister and James Parker, and Mary Archibald had her own household at Gean Tree. Six years later, when the Edinburgh registrar asked Agnes where she lived, the answer had changed.

That address is the one piece of the story that survives in Agnes's own words. Robert and Elizabeth Douglas enter the boy's story later. By the time we see him with them in Edinburgh, he is three.

The record lays it out. Her father, George Brown, died at Edston in April 1886, when she was three and a half months old. Her mother, Christina, died at Quothquan in February 1891, and her grandmother, Jane Henderson, died that June. Agnes was raised in her grandmother's cottage in the row, the house later called Lime Tree, and she was still living there with her uncle Andrew at fifteen, on census night in 1901. When her son was born in the summer of 1907, she was living a few doors along the same row, at Gean Cottage. She said so herself, in the register.
